We first derive an ionospheric activity index in percentage by comparing observed TEC values with a quiet--time reference.
To account for seasonal, diurnal, and latitudinal variations in TEC fluctuations, each percentage deviation is normalized using the robust Z--score method.
The ISS is then established by defining thresholds for the normalized data, categorizing activity into seven levels: ISS0, ISS P 1, ISS P 2, ISS P 3, ISS N 1, ISS N 2, and ISS N 3.
Results reveal that the new index exhibits no diurnal or seasonal dependence, a key requirement for a homogeneous ionospheric activity time series.

Correlation analysis between the ionospheric activity index and the residuals of the ionospheric TEC model we developed previously, along with variations in the index during geomagnetic storms, demonstrates that the ISS can serve as a reliable indicator of the expected performance of ionospheric models and well represents ionospheric activity.

Finally, analysis of the relationship between standard point positioning accuracy and the ionospheric activity index under different solar activity levels reveals that higher ionospheric activity corresponds to increased positioning errors during periods of high solar activity.

title: Geomagnetically Induced Currents, Transformer Harmonics, and Reactive Power Impacts: Observed Response of a Single-Phase Transformer in New Zealand

sentences.text: Geomagnetic storms represent a space weather hazard to power transmission networks due to the effects of induced geo-electric fields within the conducting surface of the Earth.
These drive electric currents in power transmission lines which can flow to ground through the neutral-ground connections of transformers.
Geomagnetically induced currents (GIC) can negatively impact the operation of high voltage transformers through asymmetric half-cycle transformer core saturation.

In this study GIC measurements, derived effective current, and reactive power responses (Q) of the single-phase bank autotransformer, T4, operating at 220 kV in the Halfway Bush substation, Dunedin, New Zealand have been analyzed over the period 2013─2017.
During 8 elevated GIC events linear enhancements of reactive power consumption (Q con , MVAr) occurred, even with comparatively low levels of GIC (i.e., <7 A).
This is consistent with transformer core saturation where there is little tolerance or "headroom" to GIC in the design for single-phase bank transformers.
Reactive power measurements show high variability.
The removal of the non-GIC variability is difficult and introduces uncertainty into the identification of GIC-driven responses.
In this analysis we consider two techniques to isolate GIC-induced reactive power responses.
We find that transformer T4 exhibited a reactive power response of ∼0.115 MVAr/A.
The results are a factor of 2─3 larger than MVAr changes in a nearby three-phase, three-limb autotransformer, aligning with previous research.
The results are consistent with, but less extreme than modeling studies found for transformer units operating at significantly higher voltages.

title: Global Effect of Long-Lasting 07─12 October 2024 Geomagnetic Storms During the Transition From a Strong (G3) to a Severe (G4) on the Geomagnetic Field and Ionospheric Parameters Distribution

sentences.text: This study investigates the co-evolution of geomagnetic field disturbances with ionospheric parameters and their characteristic latitudinal signatures by conducting a location and time-dependent analysis of the 07─12 October 2024 events, to fill crucial gaps in understanding the coupled response of the magnetosphere-ionosphere system.

This has been carried out utilizing integrated multi-instrument approach combining ground-based magnetometer-derived geomagnetic fields deviations from the mean (∆Bx, ∆By, ∆Bz), Digisonde-derived critical frequency and maximum electron density at the F2-ionospheric layer (foF2, hmF2), and Global Navigation Satellite System Total Electron Content (GNSS TEC) measurements.

Significant disturbances in the ∆Bx component are observed across all sectors in the low-latitude region, particularly when the storm intensity increases; while in the mid-latitude region, all magnetic field components exhibit significant disturbances across American stations.
Mid- and low-latitude stations displayed more stable but still disturbed patterns in both storm cases, with phase dependent and sector-specific ionospheric responses.

During the initial phase, prompt penetration electric fields increased TEC in low-latitude regions, particularly during evening hours (19:00─23:00 UT) when the equatorial ionization anomaly was strongest.

The American sector experienced the most pronounced and coincide geomagnetic field and ionospheric perturbations during both storms, showing the largest ∆Bx and TEC enhancements relative to quiet-time maxima.
Notably, the main phase of the 10─12 October 2024 storm resulted in the largest depletion of TEC and foF2, measured against quiet-time minima.
Larger TEC enhancements also coincides with substantial hmF2 depression and foF2 reduction than higher hmF2 and foF2 when the intensity of the storm enhances.

title: The Impact of the May 2024 Geomagnetic Storm on TRISAT Orbital Decay: A TLE-Based Analysis With a Lifetime Forecast

sentences.text: The 10─13 May 2024 geomagnetic storm was one of the strongest space-weather events of Solar Cycle 25 and produced a major expansion of the thermosphere, substantially increasing atmospheric drag on low-Earth-orbit spacecraft.

In this study, we quantify the storm-time orbital response of TRISAT, Slovenia's first 3U CubeSat, using publicly available Two-Line Element data, SWARM-C accelerometer measurements, NRLMSIS-2.1 density estimates, and European Space Agency's DRAMA/OSCAR lifetime modeling.
TLE-derived semimajor-axis variations show that TRISAT's orbital decay increased from a pre-storm baseline of about 0.4 km/day to peak values exceeding 1 km/day during the main phase of the storm.
Over 10─13 May, the semimajor axis decreased by approximately 2.5 km.

Independent density-sensitive observations from SWARM-C and empirical thermospheric modeling indicate a storm-time density enhancement of roughly a factor of 2─3, consistent with the observed acceleration of orbital decay.
Lifetime propagation with DRAMA/OSCAR further indicates that the event shortened TRISAT's remaining orbital lifetime by about 1 week over the analyzed interval.

A broader population analysis of low-Earth-orbit satellites shows that the strongest storm-time degradation occurred among low-altitude, high-drag, non-propulsive spacecraft, placing TRISAT within a particularly vulnerable class of small satellites.

These results demonstrate that short-duration geomagnetic storms can produce measurable mission-level consequences for CubeSats, including accelerated orbital decay, reduced lifetime, and degraded orbit-prediction accuracy.
Empirical thermospheric models such as NRLMSIS-2.1 reproduce the overall density enhancement but may underestimate short-term storm variability.

title: Space Weather Disrupts Low-Latitude Network RTK: Evidence From LSTIDs During June 2025 Geomagnetic Storm

sentences.text: The geomagnetic storm on 1 June 2025 generated pronounced large-scale traveling ionospheric disturbances (LSTIDs) over China, captured by dense GNSS networks.

It has been unclear whether network real-time kinematic (NRTK) positioning, which relies on spatial interpolation from multiple reference stations, remains effective under such extreme space weather conditions.
This study provides direct observational evidence that links the passage of LSTIDs to the degradation of NRTK performance in a low-latitude region.
We identified strong LSTIDs with amplitudes of ±0.4 TECU propagating equatorward at speeds of 0.3─1.3 km/s and wavelengths of 1,150─1,600 km during the storm's main phase.
These ionospheric gradients disrupted the spatial correlation assumed by the NRTK algorithm, leading to interpolation residuals exceeding 10 cm.
The largest residuals were mainly associated with satellites to the south of the user station, indicating that the LSTID impact may be modulated by satellite azimuth.
As a result, integer ambiguity resolution frequently failed, reducing the horizontal positioning accuracy to the 5─10 cm level.

These findings delineate a complete observation-based pathway from geomagnetic activity to decimeter-level positioning errors, confirming a specific vulnerability of advanced high-precision navigation infrastructure to LSTIDs during space weather events.

title: Auroral Effect on Mid-Latitude Ionospheric Disturbances Over Europe During the Extreme Geomagnetic Storm of 10 May 2024

sentences.text: Large ionospheric disturbances were observed over Europe during the extreme geomagnetic storm on 10 May 2024.
This study analyzes GNSS--derived total electron content (TEC) and all--sky imager data to investigate these disturbances.
Pronounced TEC enhancements, irregularities, and strong gradients were confined to the auroral region above the mid--latitudes.
These anomalies evolved coherently with the equatorward expansion of the optical aurora.
Large--scale TEC disturbances were found to be moving at mid--latitudes with an equatorward velocity of 726 m/s and an amplitude of up to 7 TECU.
These characteristics were indicative of the auroral expansion rather than of large--scale traveling ionospheric disturbances (LSTIDs), which exhibited weaker amplitudes near the auroral boundary.
This finding contrasts with the interpretation of some previous studies on GNSS observations.
This study demonstrates the visualization of the auroral oval at mid--latitudes using TEC and TEC--derived parameters.

title: Iono-PhyTAU: A Lightweight Global Ionospheric TEC Prediction Model Based on Temporal Attention Unit and Physical Condition Constraints of the Ionosphere

sentences.text: Ionospheric Total Electron Content (TEC) is the primary error source causing signal delay in Global Navigation Satellite Systems (GNSS).
High--precision TEC prediction is essential for positioning, navigation, and space weather monitoring.

Although deep learning models including ConvLSTM, ConvGRU, and Transformer have advanced TEC forecasting, they still struggle to capture long--range global spatiotemporal dependencies, suffer from severe error accumulation in multi--step prediction, and involve high computational cost and large parameters.
To address these limitations, this paper proposes a lightweight deep learning model called Iono--PhyTAU for global ionospheric TEC prediction.

The model integrates a Temporal Attention Unit (TAU) and external physical driving constraints, which reduces computational complexity, enhances long--sequence dependence modeling, and extracts fine--grained spatiotemporal features.
The model significantly improves TEC prediction accuracy during geomagnetic storms.

Experiments conducted in the high solar activity year (2015) and low solar activity year (2020) show that Iono--PhyTAU achieves the best prediction accuracy, with RMSE values of 2.97 TECU and 1.08 TECU, respectively.

The model effectively alleviates error accumulation in multi--step prediction: after the fourth hr of daily forecasting in 2015, its RMSE is reduced by 0.3--0.5 TECU compared with the suboptimal ConvLSTM model and by 0.5--1.5 TECU compared with C1PG.
In addition, Iono--PhyTAU exhibits strong robustness across different latitudes, seasons, and times, with particularly outstanding performance during geomagnetic storms.
Experimental results confirm that the model can adapt to various space weather environments and performs excellently in geomagnetic storm events.
It has great application potential in improving the reliability of global TEC forecasting and provides strong support for GNSS ionospheric delay correction.

title: Model-Based Analysis of Ionospheric TEC Disturbances Over China and Adjacent Regions During the May 2024 Super Geomagnetic Storm

sentences.text: This study uses observation data from multi--constellation (GPS/GLONASS/Galileo/BeiDou) ground--based Global Navigation Satellite Systems (GNSS) networks and a non--integrated spherical harmonic function modeling methodology to develop an ionospheric Total Electron Content (TEC) model with high spatiotemporal resolution (1° × 1° in longitude and latitude, and 15 min in time) over China and adjacent regions.
The response of regional ionospheric TEC during the May 2024 super geomagnetic storm was then investigated using this model.
The results indicate that the model can accurately capture the spatiotemporal variation characteristics of regional ionospheric TEC during this geomagnetic storm.
During the main and early recovery phases of the geomagnetic storm, positive and negative ionospheric disturbances occurred simultaneously.

During the late recovery phases of the storm, long--lasting negative ionospheric disturbances dominated, causing a substantial TEC decrease, with a maximum decrease of about 70 TECU and a relative decrease of up to 80%.
The daytime ionospheric TEC on 12 May was almost comparable to the typical night--time value.
Additionally, ionospheric response exhibited east--west differences.

Furthermore, during certain periods of the superstorm's recovery phase, positive ionospheric disturbances occurred against an overall negative storm background at middle and low latitudes; this non--locally generated disturbance spans 20°N--40°N with its center near 30°N (projected radius ~10°), propagates westward at ~140 ± 8 m/s, and shows no obvious spatial contraction but a gradual intensity weakening with differential total electron content decreasing from ~30 TECU to 2~3 TECU.
These phenomena indicated that the ionosphere over China and adjacent regions experienced complex variations during this super geomagnetic storm.

title: Feasibility analysis of the Doppler index DI in ionospheric scintillation detection at High Arctic region of Canada

sentences.text: Based on data from 16 ISMR stations of Canadian High Arctic Ionospheric Network (CHAIN)
this study analyses ionospheric scintillation phenomena during the strong geomagnetic storm on April 23, 2023.
The intensity and duration of the geomagnetic storm were confirmed through variations in the Dst and Kp indexes and the global TEC map.
The spatiotemporal distribution and correlation of the DI, ROTI and indexes were analysed, alongside PPP experiments at all stations.
The de-trended TEC (dTEC) analysis revealed a link between ionospheric scintillation and TEC fluctuations.

Statistical results show a correlation coefficient around 0.7─0.9 between the DI index and ROTI/ indexes, with consistent spatiotemporal distributions, especially during the main phase of the geomagnetic storms from 9:00 to 21:00 UTC.

The DI was also applied to explore the impact of ionospheric scintillation on GPS PPP, where the fluctuations in DI corresponded with increased positioning errors, highlighting its effectiveness as a monitoring tool.

title: Application of slant total electron content obtained from the computerized ionospheric tomography for Precise Point Positioning (PPP)

sentences.text: The undifferenced and uncombined precise point positioning (UPPP) method preserves ionospheric parameters as estimable variables, this methodology facilitates the integration of external ionospheric constraints.

In this study, we employ ionospheric tomography technology to obtain high-precision ionospheric products that are applied to UPPP in the forms of slant total electron content (STEC) (PPP-CIT-STEC) and vertical total electron content (VTEC) (PPP-CIT-VTEC).
In addition, the UPPP approach incorporates the 2-dimensional VTEC model (PPP-2D-VTEC).
The positioning performance of these three UPPP methods is compared and analyzed.
Using observation data from the United States and Hunan Province, experiments were conducted for GPS UPPP and BDS UPPP.

The findings revealed that PPP-CIT-STEC significantly outperformed PPP-2D-VTEC and PPP-CIT-VTEC, achieving improvements in positioning accuracy of more than 20% and 12%, and in convergence performance of more than 25% and 13%, respectively.
During the geomagnetic storm, PPP-CIT-STEC also demonstrated remarkable robustness.

This research highlights the efficacy of high-precision ionospheric products in enhancing the performance of UPPP, while also mitigating the influence of mapping functions on positioning outcomes in the computation of ionospheric delays within UPPP.

title: U-Net Based Forecasting of Storm-Time Total Electron Content over North Africa Using Assimilation of GNSS Observation into Global Ionospheric Maps

sentences.text: This study presents U-Net deep learning of total electron content (TEC) obtained from Global Ionosphere Maps (GIMs) to forecast ionospheric TEC over the African 0─40° N latitude sector during geomagnetic storms which have occurred between 2011 and 2024.

Before being utilized in the deep learning procedure, the GIM-TEC data were improved by assimilating ground-based vertical TEC (VTEC) observations from available Global Navigation Satellite System (GNSS) receiver stations.
The U-Net one-hour-ahead prediction of TEC was examined during the intense geomagnetic storm of May 2024.
Additionally, the model's accuracy and reliability were evaluated through quantitative comparison with established climatological models, including IRI-2020 and AfriTEC storm time models.
The results indicate that the integration of data assimilation with the deep learning framework yields TEC estimates that closely agree with observations, achieving a RMSE of approximately 5 TECU.
On the other hand, the IRI-2020 model exhibits substantially larger errors, with RMSE ~10─17 TECU, while the AfriTEC model shows the poorest performance, with RMSE reaching approximately 15─22 TECU.

Further, the U-Net was validated using two equatorial and mid-latitude GNSS stations whose data were excluded from the assimilation process, achieving RMSE values of 4.44 and 6.75 TECU and correlation coefficients of 0.93 and 0.97, confirming the model forecasting capability for reproducing ionospheric TEC variability.
These results establish the model as a precise, robust tool for TEC prediction in regions with sparse GPS coverage that is crucial for ionospheric monitoring and space weather applications.

title: Radio-quiet ionosonde measurements for monitoring absorption in the HF band

sentences.text: Enhancements to the D layer of the ionosphere can be produced through different mechanisms: X-ray burst from solar flares or particle impacts due to solar energetic particle events or to auroral precipitation during geomagnetic storms.
Each of these phenomena has a different source, affects a different region and play out on a different timescale.
The final result, however, is in each case an increase in the amount of absorption experienced by HF and VHF radio signals in the ionosphere.
For users of these radio bands, it is important to be aware of the level of D-layer absorption, regardless of which space weather phenomena is ultimately responsible.
There exist several methods to monitor the level of D-layer absorption, but global coverage of observations—especially those available in real-time—is still limited.
We will present a technique to monitor ionospheric absorption in the HF radio band using ionosondes.
This allows us to add real-time absorption data at the location of existing ionosondes, without the need to deploy new instrumentations.
For this purpose, the ionosondes were run in a radio-silent mode, recording not reflections of their own emitted signals but signals from transmitters of opportunity.
Such signals are ubiquitous in all but the most remote, uninhabited regions, especially in various bands reserved for broadcasting applications.
Such bands are intensively used by various users employing relatively high-powered transmitters, which can be received through ionospheric propagation at long distances.
We monitor the signal strength received through the HF band, particularly in the bands reserved for broadcasting, to determine the real-time level of signal attenuation.
We present first the quiet-time data, showing what the typical diurnal patern in the spectrograms is.
This is important as the level of signals received in various bands depends on the location of the observatory.
Absorption can therefore best be determined as a relative variation from the quiet, diurnal variations for a particular location and instrument.
Next, we present the impact of both solar flares and particle storms on the D-layer ionisation, and therefore on the level of absorption of HF radio signals.

We show that solar flares and particle events both have characteristic signatures in the radio-quiet received spectrograms, which allow real-time detection and possibly quantification of absorption enhancements.
We will present several examples observed during the major disturbances that occurred in recent years, as well as the first steps towards a quantification of impacts as a function of frequency.

title: Response of global low-latitude ionospheric irregularities during the intense magnetic storm in May 2024

sentences.text: The strongest magnetic storm since the 25th solar cycle occurred from May 10 to 14, 2024.
The storm began abruptly at 14 UT on the 10th, with a rapid and slight increase in the Dst index.
The main phase of the storm began at 17 UT, and the Dst index rapidly decreased, reaching a minimum of -406 nT at 02 UT on the 11th.
Subsequently, the recovery phase of the storm began, and the Dst index gradually recovered.
By around 20 UT on the 13th, the Dst index had returned to a level above -50
nT.
The Dst index was below -100 nT from 20 UT on the 10th to 14 UT on the 12th, lasting for 38 hours, during which the Kp index reached a maximum of 9^09^09^0.

Using observational data from the COSMIC-2 and SWARM satellites, as well as ground-based GPS observations, an analysis was conducted on the response of global low-latitude ionospheric irregularities during this intense magnetic storm.
The main results indicate that: (1) Before the occurrence of the magnetic storm, low-latitude ionospheric irregularities mainly occurred in the African region (0^∘∼60^∘).
The occurrence of the magnetic storm had significantly different impacts on ionospheric irregularities in different longitude regions.

(2) During the main phase of the storm on the 10th, a large spatial range of plasma depletion structures appeared at night in the South American-African region (-60^∘∼60^∘), accompanied by ionospheric irregularities, with the most pronounced effects in the African region.
(3) During the recovery phase of the magnetic storm on the 11th, the ionospheric irregularities in the African and Indian Ocean regions (0^∘∼100^∘) almost completely disappeared.
However, in most other longitude regions, there were obvious large-scale plasma depletion structures and enhanced ionospheric irregularity activities.

This was most pronounced in the eastern Pacific region (-180^∘ ∼-60^∘) and the western Pacific region (100^∘∼180^∘), where ionospheric irregularity activities persisted throughout the night and even into the day.

(4) During the recovery phase of the magnetic storm on the 12th and 13th, the South America-Atlantic region (-60^∘∼0^∘) still exhibited large-scale plasma depletion structures and ionospheric irregularity activities.
The ionospheric irregularity activities in the eastern Pacific region gradually weakened, while those in the western Pacific region almost completely disappeared.

The combined effects of the prompt penetration electric field and the disturbance dynamo electric field during the magnetic storm may play an important role in generating/suppressing ionospheric irregularity activities in different low-latitude regions.

title: Global Ionospheric Disturbances Induced by Solar Flares During the Main and Recovery Phases of the May 2024 Superstorm Under High Solar Activity

sentences.text: Between 10 and 17 May 2024, the solar active region AR3664 produced the most intense coronal mass ejection (CME) recorded in the past two decades, leading to geomagnetic superstorm.
During this geomagnetic superstorm, two solar flares (SFs) occurred under distinct geomagnetic conditions.
The first flare took place during the main phase of the storm (SYM-H = ─518 nT; Kp = 9), while the second occurred in the end of the recovery phase (SYM-H = ─53 nT; Kp = 2─).

In this study, ground-based magnetometer observations, together with GPS-derived vertical total electron content (VTEC) and rate of TEC (ROT) data, are used to examine the spatial and temporal electrodynamics of the ionosphere across a broad geographic region.
The analysis focuses on the ionospheric response to both solar flares, emphasizing their occurrence during different geomagnetic storm phases.
From a space weather perspective, this work provides new insights into the coupled effects of geomagnetic disturbances and Sudden Ionospheric Disturbances (SIDs) induced by solar flares.
Furthermore, variations in the equatorial electrojet (EEJ) are investigated to elucidate the electrodynamic processes operating during these extreme solar─terrestrial events.

title: Equatorial Ionospheric Response to the May 11, 2024, Geomagnetic Superstorm over Ecuador

sentences.text: This study examines how an extreme G5 geomagnetic storm affected the ionosphere over Ecuador, including the Galápagos Islands, from 10 to 13 May 2024.

We used data from multiple GPS stations to measure the Total Electron Content (TEC), which represents the number of electrons in the ionosphere and directly affects satellite communication and navigation signals.
We also monitored the horizontal component of the magnetic field, which is highly sensitive to geomagnetic disturbances.

During the storm's peak (10─11 May), the TEC decreased by about 30 TEC units, while the horizontal magnetic field dropped by more than 400 nT. This decrease in TEC, instead of the typical increase seen in some storms, was caused by storm-driven changes in the upper atmosphere that accelerated electron loss and disrupted normal ionospheric processes.
These results show that severe geomagnetic storms can strongly affect the equatorial ionosphere and emphasize the need for continuous monitoring to protect satellite-based systems.

title: Longitudinal variation of ionospheric irregularities and response of the ionosphere during May and October 2024 geomagnetic storms

abbreviations.RODI: rate of change of electron density Ne index
abbreviations.ROTI: rate of change of TEC index

sentences.text: We examine the response of the ionosphere to the May and October 2024 geomagnetic storms, the two recent great geomagnetic storms of solar cycle 25.
We identified the occurrence of ionospheric irregularities during the two geomagnetic storms.

We used percentage change in vertical total electron content (∆VTEC%) computed using VTEC data from three equatorial ground-based global navigation satellite system (GNSS) receivers in the American, African, and Asian sectors, to study the ionospheric response.

In order to determine the occurrence of ionospheric irregularities, we employed the rate of change of electron density (Ne) index (RODI) from Swarm satellite-A (Sw-A) and the rate of change of TEC index (ROTI) from the GNSS TEC.
We found that the longitudinal response to the two storms were different in terms of TEC and irregularities as a function of storm phase.
Our results revealed a positive ionospheric storm over the African and Asian sectors during the main phase of May storm; whereas a negative ionospheric response was recorded over the American sector.
In contrast, during the October storm, a positive ionospheric storm effect was observed over the American and African sectors and negatively over the Asian sector.

Additionally, we identified that the October storm had a higher percentage irregularity occurrence rate than the May storm, although the May storm's G5 level was higher than the October storm's G4 level.
All sectors experienced irregularities during the two main storms phases, with the exception of the American sector during the May 2024 storm, when an inhibition was observed.
Sw-A showed a longitudinal trend in the occurrence rate of irregularities during the May storm, with America having the lowest rate, followed by Africa and Asia.
During the October storm, this longitudinal dependence is reversed, with irregularities occurring over the America, Africa and Asia, respectively, from the highest to lowest.

The findings of this study provide the scientific community with new insights into how geomagnetic storms influence ionospheric plasma structure, occurrence of irregularities, and can help improve space weather prediction and modeling.

title: Features of ionospheric irregularities in the transitional low-to-mid latitudes observed from anomaly crest location

sentences.text: Equatorial ionospheric irregularities intersect and interfere with transionospheric radio signals often resulting in serious degradation of their performance including that of satellite-based systems and services.
While such phenomena are associated with geomagnetic disturbed conditions in the mid and high latitudes, they could occur even under geomagnetic quiet conditions in the equatorial and low latitudes.
The radio frequency signals affected also varies across a wide spectrum extending from VHF to L-band and often S-band as well.

Some novel coordinated experimental observations were recorded during February-March 2024 using University of Calcutta VHF radar operating at 53 MHz at the Ionosphere Field Station, Haringhata (22.93N, 88.37E geographic; 35N magnetic dip) and GPS L-band measurements from North Bengal University (NBU) (26.71N, 88.35E geographic; 42N magnetic dip).
The present paper reports three cases which occurred on February 23, March 18 and 28, 2024.

The Radar beam has to be directed towards the north from Haringhata in order to achieve the condition of orthogonality with the magnetic field lines around a subionospheric location of 25N, 88E. On March 18, 2024, the VHF radar backscattered signals noted a number of irregularity patches occurring around 20:30, 22:00 and 23:30 LT respectively at heights ranging from 300-650 km.
The GPS links studied from NBU were limited over a swath of 22-26.5N and 86-91E so as to observe a common ionospheric volume.
On March 18, 2024, TEC depletion was noted on the SV18 link around 24:00 LT while SV29 experienced depletions around 21:00-21:30 LT and SV32 around 23:15-23:30 LT.
Similar analyses have also been for February 23 and March 28, 2024.
These novel coordinated measurements validate the simultaneous coexistence of ionospheric irregularities of varying scale sizes ranging from centimeters to metres using the VHF radar and GPS.
However, an outstanding issue to consider is the occurrence of ionospheric irregularities even at L-band at a magnetic dip of 39N during late evening and midnight hours.
This brings forth the question whether these irregularities could be attributed to equatorial plasma bubbles or to some remnants of transitional mid-latitude plasma density structures.
Further work is underway on these aspects.

title: Unusually strong equatorial ionization anomaly across three local time sectors during the intense 10─11 May 2024 Geomagnetic Storm

sentences.text: The Earth's upper atmosphere is significantly influenced by space weather events, particularly geomagnetic storms.
In this study, we investigate the impact of an intense geomagnetic storm that occurred on 10─11 May 2024 on the equatorial and low-latitude ionosphere.
Using datasets from various ground and satellite-based (SWARM and GOLD satellites, Global GNSS receivers, Incoherent Scatter Radar, Fabry-
Perot interferometers, and magnetometers) measurements, we show the impact of extreme prompt penetration of the electric field on the development of the plasma fountain during the storm.
Prompt penetration electric field caused a significant enhancement in the ionospheric vertical drift (∼95 m/s) and the equatorial electrojet strength (∼275 nT) over Jicamarca.
These extreme eastward electric field perturbations, along with the large meridional wind, significantly altered the F-region plasma fountain at different local times.
The afternoon equatorial ionization anomaly (EIA) not only sustained for an exceptionally long duration (∼12 hr) but also expanded spatially over time.
EIA crests extended beyond ±35° MLat in both hemispheres over the Jicamarca meridian during the afternoon and evening hours, eventually merging with the aurora.

This study shows, for the first time, that unusually strong EIA can not only develop at different local times but can also sustain for long durations under favorable conditions, which has implications for space weather applications.

title: Study of an extreme space weather event in South America based on ionospheric indices

sentences.text: There are many kinds of ionospheric indices proposed to show important information about the state of the ionosphere.
Some of them are based on dual frequency GNSS carrier phase measurements.

We utilized GNSS observations from March 17-18, 2015, specifically around the time of the St. Patrick's Day geomagnetic storm and studied the behavior of the following indices: the Rate of TEC Index (ROTI), the Sudden Ionospheric Disturbance Index (SIDX), the Weather Index (W), the Disturbance Ionosphere Index (DIX) and the Ionospheric Gradient Index (GIX) during this extreme Space Weather event.
To assess the sensitivity of the indices to the different phases of the storm, the temporal behaviour of each index was analysed at different magnetic latitudes.
For the calculation of the ROTI, SIDX and DIX indices, the geometry-free combination method was used instead of VTEC values, employing all available GNSS constellations and frequency combinations.
Based on our study, we can affirm that local time and geomagnetic latitude significantly influence the ionospheric indices.
This result is related to the evolution of electrodynamic processes during the development of the magnetic storm.
A relevant outcome is the response of the indices in the different phases of the storm in the mid-latitude region.

We observe that during the positive phase of the storm, the space-time gradient increases as a result of the greater contribution of electric fields, thermospheric winds and other factors, which accelerates the increase in VTEC.
Meanwhile, during the negative phase, the overall effect of these processes on the ionosphere decreases, slowing down the growth of VTEC and, in some cases, even causing a decrease.

title: Monitoring Storm-Time Low-Latitude Ionospheric Disturbances over India Using NavIC/IRNSS

sentences.text: This study investigates low-latitude ionospheric responses over the Indian region during six intense geomagnetic storms between 2017 and 2024, including the extreme May 2024 superstorm, using NavIC/IRNSS and IGS observations.
Variations in Total Electron Content (TEC), Rate of TEC Index (ROTI), and scintillation index (S4) are analysed using data from a NavIC receiver at Sangli (16.5°N, 74.3°E) and regional GNSS stations.

The observed responses are examined in relation to interplanetary conditions, geomagnetic indices, Equatorial Electrojet (EEJ) variability, storm-time electric fields, and thermospheric composition changes (O/N₂).
CME-driven storms produced rapid daytime TEC enhancements, whereas CIR─HSS storms caused prolonged disturbances.

The May 2024 superstorm (Dst ≍ −412 nT) resulted in widespread TEC depletion with brief flare-induced enhancements, demonstrating the effectiveness of NavIC/IRNSS for monitoring storm-time ionospheric variability.

title: Ionosphere Responses during Geomagnetic Storm and Quiet Events via GNSS CM01 Receiver in Thailand

sentences.text: Ionospheric variability is a critical component of space weather, particularly in low-latitude regions near the geomagnetic equator, where ionospheric dynamics are strongly influenced by geomagnetic activity.

This study investigates ionospheric responses over Thailand during geomagnetic storm and quiet conditions in November 2025, using Total Electron Content (TEC) derived from the Global Navigation Satellite System (GNSS) CM01 receiver.
The CM01 station is located at 98^∘57^'18.9^'' E and 18^∘48^'07.94^'' N, at an altitude of 305.8 m in northern Thailand.
This near-geomagnetic-equator location makes the site well suited for examining storm-time ionospheric disturbances and equatorial plasma processes.
GNSS observations from the CM01 receiver are analyzed to characterize temporal variations in TEC during selected geomagnetic storm events and background quiet periods.

The analysis focuses on storm-time TEC enhancements and depletions, disturbance structures, and increased ionospheric irregularities, with particular attention to phenomena such as Equatorial Plasma Bubbles (EPBs).
Comparisons between disturbed and quiet conditions are conducted to isolate storm-driven ionospheric responses from background variability.

The results provide insight into the sensitivity of low-latitude ionospheric electron density to geomagnetic forcing and highlight distinct differences between storm-time and quiet-time ionospheric behavior over Thailand.

This study contributes to improved understanding of ionospheric variability in the Southeast Asian sector and supports the development of regional ionospheric monitoring and forecasting capabilities relevant to GNSS-based navigation and communication systems.
Acknowledgments This work is financially supported by the NSRF via the Program Management Unit for the Human Resources and Institutional Development, Research and Innovation (Grant no. B41G690022).

title: Performance of Low-Cost GNSS Receivers for Storm-Time Ionospheric Monitoring

sentences.text: This study evaluates the capability of low-cost multi-frequency GNSS receivers, in conjunction with geodetic-grade instruments, to monitor storm-time ionospheric variability over the Indian region.
Emphasis is placed on both receiver performance assessment and the characterization of space-weather-driven ionospheric disturbances.

Variations in Total Electron Content (TEC) and the Rate of TEC Index (ROTI) during the extreme May 2024 superstorm (Dst ≍ −412 nT) are analysed using observations from a low-cost GNSS receiver installed at Sangli (16.52°N, 74.34°E) and co-located International GNSS Service (IGS) Hyderabad (17.42°N, 78.55°E) stations.

TEC estimates obtained from the low-cost receiver show excellent agreement with geodetic-grade IGS stations observations, with correlation coefficients exceeding 0.9, demonstrating robust performance even under severely disturbed geomagnetic conditions.

The May 2024 superstorm produced pronounced and widespread TEC depletion over low latitudes, primarily associated with dominant westward prompt-penetration electric fields and suppressed upward E×B drift.
In contrast, short-lived TEC enhancements were observed in response to X-class solar flares.
The timing and magnitude of post-flare TEC responses during the May 2024 superstorm and the November 2025 event (Dst ≍ −217 nT) are also examined.

Overall, the results confirm that low-cost multi-frequency GNSS receivers provide reliable TEC and ROTI measurements during extreme space-weather events, highlighting their strong potential for continuous storm-time ionospheric monitoring and space-weather applications in low-latitude regions.
Keywords: Low-cost GNSS receiver; Total Electron Content (TEC); Geomagnetic storms; Ionospheric variability; ROTI; Space weather

title: Monitoring Ionospheric Changes on Horseshoe Island, Antarctica: A Case Study of the May 12, 2021 Geomagnetic Storm

sentences.text: The high-latitude ionosphere is one of the most susceptible regions to energetic particle precipitation resulting from solar activities and geomagnetic storms, primarily due to open magnetic field lines.
This vulnerability renders every study conducted in the region both critical and characteristic.

In this context, ionospheric variations over the polar region are systematically monitored using data from the TUR1 GNSS station, operated within the Turkish Scientific Research Camp located on Horseshoe Island, Antarctica.
This study focuses on the geomagnetic activity event recorded on May 12, 2021 (DOY 132), during the ascending phase of the onset of Solar Cycle 25.

Within the scope of the study, Total Electron Content (TEC) estimations were performed using high-resolution RINEX observation data obtained from the TUR1 station, and ROTI (Rate of TEC Index) values—a key indicator of ionospheric irregularities were calculated.

Through the analysis of the DOY 132 case, electron density fluctuations occurring in the ionospheric F layer due to the geomagnetic storm and the impact of these fluctuations on GNSS signal quality were investigated.
Furthermore, the hardware performance and signal tracking sensitivity of the TUR1 station were evaluated based on the variations in the Signal-to-Noise Ratio (SNR) recorded during the storm.
The results demonstrate that on DOY 132, when the Kp index reached 4+, significant increases and abrupt fluctuations in TEC values were observed compared to quiet days.

These findings confirm that the TUR1 station clearly captured the increase in local ionospheric electron density (positive ionospheric storm effect) at the onset of the geomagnetic disturbance and possesses sufficient sensitivity to detect micro-scale ionospheric turbulence.

Consequently, it has been verified that the data provided by the TUR1 station constitutes a reliable, sustainable, and scientifically high-quality resource for space weather monitoring activities in the region.
"This study was supported by projects numbered "124G057" and "118Y322" within the scope of TÜBİTAK Kutup (Polar) 1001 program."
The authors thanks TUBITAK for their support.
Keywords:
Ionosphere, Total Electron Content (TEC), Geomagnetic Storm, GNSS

title: Ionospheric Response to the 17 March 2015 Geomagnetic Storm over Rabat (Morocco) Using GNSS-Derived TEC

sentences.text: We investigate the ionospheric response to the geomagnetic storm of 17 March 2015 using Global Navigation Satellite System (GNSS) total electron content (TEC) measurements from the International GNSS Service (IGS) station RABT located in Rabat, Morocco (34^∘N, 7^∘W).
This storm, which reached a minimum SYM-H index of $−233 nT was the most intense geomagnetic event of solar cycle 24.
Vertical TEC (VTEC) was derived from dual-frequency pseudorange observations using a single-layer ionospheric mapping function with an assumed shell height of 350 km.

A consistent preprocessing strategy was applied, including satellite- and receiver-specific Differential Code Bias (DCB) corrections, and a minimum elevation cutoff of 30^∘ to mitigate multipath and mapping errors.

The results reveal a pronounced ionospheric enhancement during the storm main phase, with ∆VTEC reaching a maximum of 45.78 TECU on 17 March, corresponding to a 158% increase relative to the quiet-day baseline value of 28.92 ± 12.91 TECU.

Correlation analysis indicates the strongest relationship between Kp and ∆VTEC at a lag of approximately three hours (r= 0.53 during storm periods), suggesting a delayed ionospheric response to geomagnetic forcing.

These results contribute to a better understanding of mid-latitude ionospheric dynamics during extreme space-weather events and highlight the potential impacts on GNSS-based positioning and navigation systems in the European─African sector.

title: Detection and analysis of traveling ionospheric disturbances at mid-latitudes over Europe using a combination of GNSS and all-sky imager observations

sentences.text: The ionosphere, a highly dynamic region of the Earth's atmosphere, is constantly shaped by solar activity.
During geomagnetic storms, ionospheric phenomena can significantly affect technological infrastructure on Earth and in near-Earth space.
Traveling ionospheric disturbances (TIDs) are one of the manifestations of this increased geomagnetic activity.
This research focuses on detecting and identifying the large- and medium-scale TIDs occurring at mid-latitudes, over the central European sector.
Since 2023, we have analyzed several events to identify the conditions under which TIDs form and their propagation characteristics.

In this study, we combine observations from a dense network of Global Navigation Satellite System (GNSS) receivers with simultaneous measurements collected by an all-sky imaging camera located at Zugspitze in southern Germany.
We analyze total electron content (TEC), TEC anomalies and the rate of TEC index (ROTI), comparing them to the spatial and temporal propagation of airglow emissions.
The camera records nocturnal airglow and auroral emissions at 557.7, 630.0, and 777.4 nm wavelengths, enabling the investigation of ionospheric structures at various altitudes.
Our results demonstrate a high degree of consistency between GNSS-based and optical observations.

Furthermore, all-sky imaging provides more in-depth analysis of the physical and chemical characteristics of disturbances, including their height, the emitting species responsible for the observed airglow, and the relationship between TIDs and auroral activity.
Our results obtained contributed to a better understanding of ionospheric variability and its impact on radio wave propagation and GNSS-based systems during disturbed geomagnetic conditions.
This, in turn, improved the characterization of mid-latitude TIDs.

title: Estimation of the ionization rate of the ionosphere during X-class solar flares

sentences.text: Solar flares are one of the most intense space weather events affecting the Earth's ionosphere.

Increased X-ray and ultraviolet radiation fluxes during flares lead to a sharp increase in the ionization of the neutral atmosphere and, consequently, a significant increase in the electron concentration.
The occurrence of such sudden ionospheric disturbances affects the propagation of shortwave radio waves and can cause disruptions in communication and navigation systems.
Instrumental methods for studying the state and dynamics of the ionosphere make it possible to detect the emergence of ionospheric irregularities and determine their main characteristics.
However, existing experimental data are insufficient for a comprehensive analysis of the processes occurring in various ionospheric layers during solar flares.

In this study, experimental and theoretical methods were used to assess the impact of solar flare electromagnetic radiation on the state and dynamics of the Earth's ionosphere in the altitude range of 60─600 km.

Using the empirical solar radiation model (FISM2) and the neutral atmosphere model (NRLMSISE-00) as an example for two X-class flares that occurred on September 6, 2017, vertical ionization rate profiles were calculated.

The calculated results were compared with experimental data on the total electron content of the ionosphere, obtained using a GNSS receiver located at the Mikhnevo mid-latitude geophysical observatory.

It was found that the combination of empirical models allows for a qualitative assessment of the temporal dynamics of the increase in the ionization rate, and the observed excess of calculated data over measured results may be due to the influence of recombination processes not accounted for in the calculations.
The results obtained confirm the validity of the proposed approaches and open up opportunities for further research in this area.
The research was supported by the Ministry of Science and Higher Education of the Russian Federation (project registration number 122032900175-6).

title: Photonics Enabling Next Generation Magnetograph Networks

sentences.text: Space weather poses increasing risks to national security, satellite operations, power grids, aviation, and global communications, driven by solar activity such as coronal mass ejections (CMEs) and flares.
Current and planned magnetograph networks are based on expensive and bulky designs which impose limits on hemispheric coverage.

The IPSOS (Imaging Photonic Spectropolarimeter for Observing the Sun) solar magnetograph is a transformative, compact instrument that offers the possibility of re-imagining how they might be used and distributed.
In this talk, we review the current and expected future state of the IPSOS instrument and discuss its role in measuring the full vector field of the Sun at unprecedented accuracy.

The resulting observations could finally resolve questions on how the solar magnetic field is generated by the solar dynamo and the major space weather it drives: from the 22-year magnetic cycle that modulates total solar irradiance, to global coronal magnetic fields that structure the solar wind, to magnetic eruptions from sunspot active regions that power coronal mass ejections triggering major geomagnetic storms.

title: Storm-Time Thermospheric Density Enhancements During Solar Cycle 25: Multi-Level Orbitography and Implications for Space Debris Dynamics

sentences.text: The ascending and maximum phases of Solar Cycle 25 have been marked by a sequence of intense solar flares and fast coronal mass ejections (CMEs), producing several major geomagnetic storms and significant perturbations of the near-Earth space environment.

Among the most impactful events are the geomagnetic storms of February 3─4, 2022 (associated with the loss of multiple Starlink satellites), April 23─24, 2023, the severe storm of May 10─11, 2024—one of the strongest of the current cycle—and additional extreme disturbances observed in March and October 2025 near solar maximum.
These events led to substantial thermospheric heating and rapid density enhancements in low Earth orbit (LEO), dramatically increasing atmospheric drag and altering satellite and debris trajectories.

This contribution aims to establish a quantitative bridge between major solar events and thermospheric total density variations, as revealed by satellite orbitography, with a particular emphasis on implications for space debris dynamics.
The study is based on two complementary orbitographic approaches.
The first approach relies on precise orbit determination of laser-ranged geodetic satellites, including Starlette ( 800 km altitude), Stella ( 800 km), Ajisai ( 1490 km), and LARES ( 1450 km).
Their orbits are reconstructed over short arcs using Satellite Laser Ranging (SLR) data accumulated by the global network of the International Laser Ranging Service (ILRS).
The combined measurements from multiple stations worldwide allow centimeter-level orbit reconstruction with high temporal resolution.

During geomagnetic storms, short-arc solutions make it possible to identify rapid variations in non-gravitational accelerations and to retrieve equivalent thermospheric density changes with near-minute resolution.
This deterministic framework provides a highly sensitive reference for characterizing storm-time drag at specific altitudes relevant to debris populations.
The second approach exploits extended time series of Two-Line Element (TLE) data.

Although limited to kilometer-level accuracy, TLE datasets offer two key advantages: they enable individual trajectory analyses of objects with sufficiently high area-to-mass ratios, revealing storm-time semi-major axis decay, and they allow statistical investigations over large populations of operational satellites and debris fragments in LEO and MEO.
Long-term orbital adjustments and propagations are performed to characterize the cumulative impact of geomagnetic storms on orbital energy loss and lifetime reduction.
The objectives of the study are threefold.
First, we identify major solar and geomagnetic events from 2022 to 2025 that significantly modified thermospheric density at satellite altitudes.
Second, we quantify the corresponding orbital signatures using both centimeter-level SLR orbitography or long-term TLE-based analyses.

Third, we investigate the physical drivers of the observed drag enhancement, focusing on (i) the satellite's local solar time (LST), which modulates thermospheric response through day─night asymmetries, and (ii) selected solar proxies used as inputs to thermospheric density models (e.g., F10.7 flux and geomagnetic indices).
From a space debris perspective, storm-time density enhancements can temporarily accelerate orbital decay, modify conjunction statistics, and significantly alter predicted re-entry timelines.
While increased drag may contribute to debris mitigation at certain altitudes, it also introduces short-term uncertainties in orbit prediction and collision risk assessment.

The comparison between high-precision SLR-based density retrievals and large-scale TLE statistical behavior provides insight into the reliability of current thermospheric models for debris environment forecasting during extreme space-weather conditions.

Preliminary results indicate that severe geomagnetic storms produce rapid density increases clearly detectable in centimeter-level orbit reconstructions, while TLE-based analyses reveal broader population-level trends.

The amplitude of drag enhancement appears strongly dependent on local solar time, suggesting that global geomagnetic indices alone cannot capture the full spatio-temporal variability of storm-time density response.

These findings underline the necessity of improved storm-time thermospheric modeling for robust debris propagation, operational orbit determination, and long-term sustainability of the near-Earth space environment during periods of intense solar activity.

title: Altitude-dependent tracking degradation during the 19th January 2026 geomagnetic storm: implications for Starlink's orbital lowering strategy

sentences.text: Space activity is accelerating rapidly, with almost 15,000 active satellites currently in Low Earth Orbit (LEO).
As launch rates continue to rise, accurately tracking objects in space is critical for collision avoidance and space safety.
Two-Line Element (TLE) sets, orbital element data made publicly available by the US Space Command, are updated by tracking systems and use SGP4 to model satellite trajectories.
A significant drop in TLE update frequency indicates tracking degradation ─
a reduced ability to locate objects, and in severe cases a complete loss of tracking.

This becomes particularly challenging during geomagnetic storms, where interaction between solar activity, Earth's magnetic field and atmosphere causes quick, unpredictable changes that perturb satellite trajectories and compromise tracking ability.
Atmospheric drag also increases dramatically within hours, yet predictive models struggle to capture this variability.
This means we become more reliant on frequent tracking updates precisely when tracking systems are least able to provide them.

Between 19 ─ 24 January 2026, an X1.9 solar flare followed by a coronal mass ejection (CME) produced the strongest (S4) solar radiation storm since the 2003 Halloween storm, with proton flux levels exceeding 104 Protons/(cm^2 s sr) for particles above 10 MeV and a Kp index over 8.
Coinciding with this, SpaceX initiated a large-scale altitude migration of over 4,000 Starlink satellites, from approximately 550km to 480km for the purpose of space safety.
This convergence of a major space weather and major operational event makes this period a relevant case study.
This study investigates the impact of this storm on tracking ability for all active LEO satellites across January 2026, separated into 7 altitude bands ranging from 300 - 2000km.

Per band, we examine metrics including TLE update frequency (TLEs per satellite per day), semi-major axis evolution, and orbital decay rate across three time periods (before, during and after the storm).
This enables quantifying altitude-dependent tracking degradation across LEO.
For the Starlink constellation specifically, we assess evidence of the orbit lowering manoeuvres and whether the storm accelerated, decelerated or disrupted the migration.

We also examine how lower altitudes affects station-keeping propellant requirements, manoeuvre budget, and satellite lifetime, providing insight into the long-term operational consequences of this migration strategy.
As we transition out of a solar maximum, characterising how geomagnetic storms affect tracking across altitudes is essential for understanding satellite responses to storm-driven perturbations.

With mega-constellations growing in scale and undergoing large operational changes, this work will draw conclusions that inform future strategies for commercial satellite management, with direct implications for collision avoidance and long-term space safety.

title: Advancing Ionospheric Mapping and Forecasting through Probabilistic Deep Learning

sentences.text: The ionosphere represents the ionized region of Earth's upper atmosphere, acting as a highly dynamic interface between our planet and the near-Earth space environment.
Its variability, driven by solar activity and geomagnetic disturbances, poses significant challenges for global navigation and satellite communication.
Accurate characterization of the Total Electron Content (TEC) is essential for supporting space weather monitoring and mitigating navigation errors.
However, traditional models often struggle to capture small-scale variations or provide reliable confidence metrics during extreme space weather events.
This presentation provides an overview of our recent progress in developing deep learning (DL) frameworks designed to enhance ionospheric monitoring and prediction.
Central to our work is the integration of Uncertainty Quantification (UQ).

By employing deep ensembles, Bayesian layers, and transformer-based architectures, our models generate high-resolution global products that provide both precise TEC estimates and their associated predictive uncertainties.

We demonstrate that these uncertainty metrics are not merely diagnostic but provide useful information when correcting single-frequency GNSS observations for ionospheric effects, leading to reduced positioning errors.
Furthermore, we discuss the integration of multi-source data, including GNSS, satellite altimetry, and radio occultation, to mitigate spatial data sparsity, particularly over oceanic regions.
Beyond vertical TEC mapping, we introduce direct slant modeling, which eliminates the need for assumptions regarding electron density distribution ─
a common limitation in traditional approaches.

Overall, these developments demonstrate that deep learning is an exceptionally powerful and versatile tool for improving the quality and reliability of ionospheric products in space weather and navigation applications.

title: Radiation Monitors for Space weather onboard Japan Meteorological satellite "Himawari 10" in GEO

sentences.text: Continuous monitoring of energetic electrons and protons across a broad energy range has not yet been established in geostationary orbit over Japan.
This lack of sustained observations remains one of the major obstacles to accurately evaluating radiation‑induced anomalies in spacecraft.

To continuously monitors the space environment and establish accurate assessment of the radiation-induced anomalies, the Radiation Monitors for Space weather (RMS) will be installed on the upcoming geostationary meteorological satellite, Himawari 10.
RMS provides decade-long measurements of the radiation environment at the geostationary orbit over Japan.
RMS consists of two energetic‑electron monitors (RMS‑e1 and RMS-e2), one energetic‑proton monitor (RMS‑p), and a dedicated data‑processing unit (RMS‑dpu).
RMS‑e1 and RMS‑e2, mounted on the north‑ and west‑facing panels of Himawari‑10, measure electrons from 50 keV to 6 MeV.

These observations provide critical information for understanding energetic‑electron environments responsible for deep and internal charging, a major driver of discharge‑related anomalies inside spacecraft.
RMS‑p, installed on the west‑facing panel, measures protons from 10 MeV to 1 GeV.
These measurements enable observations for solar energetic particles (SEPs) associated with solar flares and galactic cosmic rays (GCRs).
Such energetic protons can induce single‑event effects (SEEs), including SEU, SET, and SEL, which may lead to critical failures in spacecraft systems.
Himawari‑10 will downlink one‑second electron and proton spectra to ground stations, and the data will be immediately transferred to NICT facilities via the ground network.
RMS also generates list‑mode data for individual particle events.
Because event rates can occasionally exceed the available telemetry bandwidth, the RMS‑dpu incorporates 2 GB of flash memory to buffer data and prevent loss during temporary burst periods.
The RMS dataset will support not only space‑weather operational services but also scientific studies of radiation‑belt electron dynamics and SEP and GCR phenomena.
Himawari‑10 is scheduled for launch in 2030, with in‑orbit observations planned through 2040.
Initial on‑orbit calibration will be performed through comparison with measurements from Arase and GOES.

title: Aviation Radiation Mitigation Strategy Validation

sentences.text: The validation of a strategy for aviation radiation hazard mitigation in development for decades has been completed using two commercial airline flights in 2024 and 2025.

This article provides a historical review of the primary elements leading to that strategy, including the emergence of aviation radiation awareness and collaborative efforts by global aviation and radiological bodies that established mitigation standards.
The primary radiation sources, galactic cosmic rays (GCRs) and solar energetic particles (SEPs), and their mechanisms of impact on Earth's atmosphere are summarized.
The article highlights the biological effects of radiation exposure influenced by altitude, latitude, and geomagnetic conditions, upon aircrew, frequent flyers, and commercial space travelers.
It recognizes a recent SWAG user needs survey report that identifies the need for continuous monitoring and predictive models to ensure long-term occupational and public health safety.
With this backdrop the validation of an ALARA-based strategy was accomplished using two UAL 990 flights on B777-200 aircraft between San Francisco and Paris.
Each carried the same ARMAS FM7 radiation monitoring unit, where one flight occurred during the extreme geomagnetic storm (Gannon storm)
May 10─11, 2024 and one flight occurred during quiet geomagnetic conditions June 8─9, 2025.
The flights' results validated the strategy during extreme space weather, i.e., by applying operational controls for shielding to reduce dose.
One approach is flying lower magnetic latitudes to gain more Earth magnetic field shielding and the other is flying lower altitudes to use atmosphere depth shielding.
Both ALARA shielding methods are controllable in airline operations and air traffic management.
These have now been validated with total dose measurements by ARMAS.
This study shows the effectiveness of the strategy to deviate flight paths to lower magnetic latitude routes and lower altitudes during major geomagnetic storms.
Not only does this approach mitigate HF communication outages but it also reduces risks from increased GNSS errors for take-off and landing navigation.
Magnetic field shielding is a major risk reduction factor for radiation, communication, and navigation while altitude shielding reduces radiation hazard risks.

title: A comprehensive analysis of the May 2024 'great' geomagnetic storm: from solar origin to near-Earth impacts

sentences.text: The great geomagnetic storm of May 10─16, 2024—driven primarily by a series of coronal mass ejections (CMEs) from Active Region (AR) 13664—was the most intense geomagnetic event in over two decades, capturing widespread scientific and public attention.
The event was further compounded by a solar energetic particle (SEP) event beginning on May 11, classified as a ground-level enhancement (GLE).
The effects of these space weather events on space assets and humans can be varied and complex, depending on both time and location.
During May 10-16, 2024, the main impacts included the severe geomagnetic storm in geospace and space radiation from SEPs.
Such an intense geomagnetic storm can have numerous potentially harmful effects, including disruptions to power grids, navigation, communication systems, and satellite altitude/attitude control.
It can also increase satellite drag, complicating precise orbit determination and collision avoidance efforts, and cause charging effects on satellite components.
SEPs can lead to single-event effects on space hardware, pose radiation risks to humans in space, and affect avionics and aviation operations.
Summary of actual impacts will be presented.

We employ tools, models, and resources available at the Community Coordinated Modeling Center (CCMC) to analyze this storm from a system-science perspective, tracing its evolution from solar origin through propagation to its effects on the near-Earth environment, with particular emphasis on inner magnetosphere dynamics.
Finally, we discuss what constitutes a 'great' solar storm from impact perspectives.

title: Lessons-learned from November 2025 and January 2026 events: impacts, gap-analysis and future recommendations

sentences.text: The recent space weather events of late 2025 and early 2026 provided a timely emphasis on the continuous need for global space weather monitoring throughout the descending phase of the solar cycle.
These events can be used as a practical stress test for aviation operations, satellite services, and power grid resilience.
This work presents a case study of the November 2025 and the January 2026 events, comparing their physical drivers, space weather impacts and operational implications.

While both events relate to the arrival of fast Earth-directed coronal mass ejections (CMEs), the events differ in severity of the accompanying solar energetic particle flux levels and induced geomagnetic activity.

The November 2025 event was characterized by a series of high-energy solar proton enhancements associated with major solar flares and fast CMEs, resulting in elevated radiation levels at aviation altitudes, degradation of high-frequency (HF) communications in polar regions, and likely increased single-event upsets in satellite systems.

The recommendations for the airlines operating polar routes in such cases are to consider altitude adjustments and rerouting strategies in accordance with space weather advisories, while for satellite operators this event is expected to trigger mitigation protocols to safeguard sensitive components.
The January 2026 event was driven by the arrival of a fast ICME and the passage of a magnetic structure with an unusually strong interplanetary magnetic field.
This led to close to extreme geomagnetic storms with associated HF COM degradation in the polar regions.

It is expected to have resulted in geomagnetically induced currents (GICs), posing concerns about power grid stability and possible intermittent disruptions to power transmission infrastructure at high latitudes.
Both events have resulted in expected GNSS signal degradation with the event in January having particularly strong impacts on the wide-area augmentation systems widely used by the aviation community.
The events have also brought beautiful auroras down to Europe.
In this study we will present a brief analysis of these two events, showing the related arrival and impact forecasts.
We will present the space weather advisories sent to aviation sector and discuss how they agree with actual impacts.
We will use that comparison to built on future recommendations for the service provision.

title: Swarm gradient products NeGIX and TEGIX for ionospheric perturbation monitoring and modeling studies

sentences.text: Accurate forecasting of ionospheric perturbations is essential for the reliable operation of trans-ionospheric radio systems such as Global Navigation Satellite Systems (GNSS), GNSS augmentation services, and space-based remote sensing.

Beyond the detection of disturbed conditions, users increasingly require quantitative information on the strength, spatial scale, and temporal evolution of ionospheric variability across low, mid, and high latitudes.

While ionospheric indices provide an efficient means of condensing complex plasma dynamics into actionable parameters, most established indices rely on ground-based GNSS observations and suffer from limited coverage over oceans and sparsely instrumented regions.

In this contribution, we present recent advances in space-based ionospheric gradient indices derived from the ESA Swarm constellation, with a focus on their relevance for ionospheric monitoring and forecast-oriented applications.

Two ionospheric indices — the electron density gradient index (NeGIX), based on in-situ Langmuir probe measurements, and the TEC gradient Index (TEGIX), derived from Swarm GNSS Precise Orbit Determination data — have been part of the Swarm operational product suite since early 2025.

By exploiting the near-parallel orbits of Swarm satellites A and C, these indices quantify horizontal plasma gradients at medium spatial scales ( 30─200 km) and resolve both meridional and zonal components in the topside ionosphere.

Although the Swarm products are not yet available in near-real-time, recent improvements in data dissemination have reduced the effective latency to approximately 8 hours, significantly enhancing their applicability for low-latency monitoring, post-event analysis, and the validation of forecast and nowcast models.

Using more than a decade of Swarm observations, we summarize validation results for quiet conditions, seasonal climatology, and severe geomagnetic storms, including recent extreme events of Solar Cycle 25.
The indices robustly capture key ionospheric structures such as the equatorial ionization anomaly dynamics, mid-latitude ionization fronts, and high-latitude patchy perturbations.

During major storms, NeGIX and TEGIX reveal strong amplification, latitudinal expansion, and pronounced asymmetries of ionospheric gradients, providing quantitative measures of perturbation intensity and spatial extent across different latitude regimes.
Comparisons with established ground-based indices (e.g. GIX) demonstrate consistency, while highlighting the unique contribution of space-based gradients in regions lacking dense GNSS coverage.

We discuss how these Swarm-based ionospheric gradient indices complement existing ground-based methods and provide a space-based relevant database for ionospheric models, studies of perturbation propagation, and the development of future index-based approaches toward forecasting ionospheric disturbances.
In this context, these Swarm gradient indices represent a valuable bridge between scientific characterization and emerging operational needs in space weather monitoring and prediction.

title: Space Weather Canada: Recent Advances in Monitoring

sentences.text: Canada has a complex magnetic environment and is among the countries most affected by space weather.

With a long history of magnetic field observations, the government run network of geomagnetic observatories is operated by the Canadian Hazards Information Service (CHIS), Natural Resources Canada (NRCan).
Currently, the network consists of 14 active stations which cover polar cap, auroral and sub-auroral latitudes and provide real time data used for monitoring and forecasting of geomagnetic activity.

While the space weather community uses various geomagnetic activity indices, such as the widely used 3-hour planetary K-index (Kp), for over 40 years Space Weather Canada (CHIS, NRCan) uses an hourly range index (HR) to describe local geomagnetic conditions across Canada.
This index is based on ranges of horizontal magnetic field components during each UT hour.
Recently, we undertook modernization of the geomagnetic forecast and explored improvements in the Canadian indices and activity scales.
This includes potential use of a running-hourly range (rHR) index, which is based on ranges of horizontal components in a sliding one hour interval window.
This sliding window can take minute steps and is better suited for real time geomagnetic activity monitoring.
Moreover, the rHR index can better capture the magnitude of magnetic field variations than the HR index.
Here, we examine data from the geomagnetic observatory network for 1973-2025, compare HR and rHR indices, and perform statistical analysis of activity to improve the geomagnetic activity scale.

Geomagnetic activity monitoring and forecasting has been a cornerstone of Space Weather Canada's work since 1970s, particularly in the aftermath of the March 1989 geomagnetic storm and the Hydro-Québec blackout.
During the last decade significant efforts were undertaken to include and expand monitoring of ionospheric conditions.

Over the last two decades, the CHIS network has expanded to include riometers to monitor ionospheric absorption and degradation in High-Frequency (HF) communications, and more recently Global Navigation Satellite System (GNSS) receivers to monitor ionospheric scintillations.
Densification of the riometer and GNSS receiver network is ongoing across the country.
Here, we report on the development of regional disturbance indicators that characterize ionospheric activity as it pertains to absorption and scintillation.

title: Ground-Based Observations and Modelling of Geomagnetically Induced Currents During the January 2026 Storm

sentences.text: Geomagnetic disturbances (GMDs) associated with solar storms can produce large geoelectric fields at Earth's surface, driving near-DC currents through the conductive ground and long infrastructure such as power transmission networks.

These geomagnetically induced currents (GICs) are of particular concern for electric power systems because they can cause half-cycle transformer saturation, excessive heating, voltage instability, and, in extreme cases, widespread service disruption.

A unique academia─industry collaboration among the University of Alberta, AltaLink L.P., ATCO Electric, and the Alberta Electric System Operator has established an integrated ground-based observational and modelling framework to investigate GICs in Alberta, Canada.

We combine transformer neutral-to-ground GIC measurements, high-resolution magnetometer observations, geoelectric field modelling using three-dimensional Earth conductivity structure, and a detailed DC equivalent power grid model.
During the geomagnetic storm of January 19-20, 2026, the peak measured GIC reached ∼75

A/phase in central Alberta, exceeding the ∼55 A/phase recorded at the same substation during the more globally intense May 2024 superstorm, despite the latter having a substantially stronger storm-time disturbance index.

This comparison demonstrates that the spatio-temporal scale of the GMD, geoelectric field orientation, subsurface conductivity, and power network topology jointly affect the GIC flowing through a given portion of the electric power network.
We observe that across multiple geomagnetic storms, some of the largest measured GICs occur consistently in central Alberta.
At the same time, modelling indicates similarly elevated GIC in northeastern Alberta, reflecting strong influence by geophysical factors and network topology.

We further evaluate an operational grid reconfiguration implemented immediately before the start of the January 2026 storm - reconnection of a high-voltage transmission line serving northern Alberta - to assess its influence on GIC through comparative simulations.

These results highlight the critical role of coordinated ground-based observation and modelling in characterizing regional space-weather risk, demonstrating how data-driven analysis can support operational mitigation strategies for power-grid resilience.

title: Potential impact of space weather effects on the variability in selected parameters characterizing Polish National Power System during the geomagnetic storm of 14 November 2012

sentences.text: We analyze the moderate geomagnetic storm of 14 November 2012 potential impact on the variability in selected parameters characterizing Polish National Power System.
We utilize anonymized, standardized hourly transmission data with the solar wind and heliospheric parameters with the geomagnetic indices.
Cross-correlation methods revealed the strongest correlation, r = 0.74, between a current-harmonic component and the Dst-index at a lag of −8 hours.
The most noticeable anti-correlation, with r = −0.66, occurred between current harmonics and the Ap-index at lags of −9 to −11 hours during a storm interval that reached minimal values of Dst-index.
Principal Component Analysis and Hierarchical Agglomerative Clustering demonstrated that seven principal components captured almost 90% of the variance.
Our results indicated that moderate storms can match with measureable changes in power-transfer and harmonic-related parameters of power system, underlining the need for multi-event studies.
This investigation proves that space weather may contribute to observable variability in the Polish power network.

title: The SupraThermal Ion Sensor (STIS) onboard the Space weather Observations at L1 to Advance Readiness 1 (SOLAR-1) spacecraft: The newest solar wind particle capability of the United States Space Weather Program

abbreviations.SOLAR-1: Space weather Observations at L1 to Advance Readiness 1

sentences.text: The Space weather Observations at L1 to Advance Readiness 1 (SOLAR-1) spacecraft is the newest space weather satellite of the United States National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA).
It was launched on September 24, 2025, and it is currently stationed in a stable orbit around the Sun-Earth Lagrange 1 (L1) point.
It is planned to become operational in the spring of 2026.
It is designed to deliver real-time observations of the solar corona to help improve forecasts of solar events that can impact Earth.

These include coronal mass ejections (CMEs) and other plasma structures emanating from the solar atmosphere, as well as the geomagnetic storms resulting from the interaction of CMEs with the Earth's magnetosphere.
The storms may induce numerous space weather effects, including power grid outages, satellite communication disruptions, and radiation harmful to humans in space.
One of the instruments onboard SOLAR-1 is the SupraThermal Ion Sensor (STIS).
STIS has two telescopes, one for electrons and one for ions, both equipped with solid state detectors that measure electrons in the range 25-250 keV, and ions in the range 25-6000 keV.
Both telescopes have an 80° x 60° Field-of-View (FOV) pointing at 50° from the Sun direction, on the ecliptic and along the Parker spiral.
The main purpose of STIS is to measure gradual Energetic Ion Enhancements (EIEs) that result from solar wind plasma acceleration by an interplanetary shock as it propagates out from the Sun.

The Space Weather Prediction Center (SWPC) monitors the flux enhancements at 47-68 keV in order to provide an advance warning of an incoming geomagnetic storm (several hours to a day), as opposed to the actual detection of the shock at L1 in the magnetic field and plasma, which gives only 10s of minutes of advanced warning.
