The STIS data products consist of differential particle fluxes with 2-s cadence plus 1-min averages provided by NOAA's National Center for Environmental Information (NCEI) and used for space weather alerts by SWPC.
In this presentation we discuss the calibration/validation steps taken to ensure accurate and reliable STIS products for operational and scientific use.

title: Solar Flare Prediction and Intensity Estimation Using a Multi-Task Transformer Encoder

sentences.text: GPS navigation, High Frequency communications, and Automated Dependent Surveillance (ADSB) are adversely impacted by solar flare activity on Earth.

A dual output transformer network has been developed that predicts the occurrence and intensity of solar flares based on sequences of magnetograms (the graphical representation of the magnetic field around the Sun).
By employing the multi-head self attention mechanism to model the behavior of the solar magnetic field, time-dependent patterns in the solar magnetic field data are effectively captured.

The experimental results demonstrate that M-class solar flares can be forecast and Xray flux can be estimated, which will allow aviation authorities to make decisions regarding/reallocate flight frequencies, provide back-up navigation, and issue Transpolar Route advisories.
For operational space weather applications, the transformer architecture outperforms conventional forecasting and machine learning methods.

title: Machine Learning-Based Prediction of Space Weather Effects on Internet Performance and GNSS Reliability

sentences.text: Space phenomena such as solar flares, coronal mass ejections, solar wind variations, geomagnetic disturbances, and ionospheric irregularities often have direct effects on Earth's communication networks.
These effects mainly include degradation of internet performance and inaccuracies in Global Navigation Satellite System (GNSS).

This paper proposes a machine-learning framework that helps to predict the effects of these space weather on internet latency, packet loss, Border Gateway Protocol (BGP) routing stability, and GNSS positioning accuracy.
The system takes space weather observations from NASA and NOAA and combines them with geospatial data which is fed as inputs to machine-learning models to predict the risks.
A dashboard analysis is also provided which helps with visualising effects on a colour-coded world map, time-series trends and solar weather timeline.
The results demonstrate the feasibility of forecasting space weather-induced disruptions using a machinelearning framework.

title: Mitigating the Impact of Geomagnetically-Induced Currents on Transformer Differential Protection

sentences.text: Faults within the transformer protection zone must be promptly cleared to prevent system instability and equipment damage.
However, geomagnetically induced currents (GIC) can cause transformer saturation and harmonic distortion, leading to misoperation or desensitization of differential protection schemes.
This paper evaluates the effectiveness of waveshape-based unblocking as an auxiliary function to enhance the sensitivity and dependability of transformer differential protection under GIC conditions.

A hardware-in-the-loop (HIL) setup was used, incorporating a commercial relay and a validated 500/230 kV transformer model connected to a reduced equivalent of Dominion Energy Virginia's transmission grid.

Through 2,322 real-time simulations across various fault types, fault resistances, and GIC magnitudes, the study demonstrates that waveshape-based unblocking significantly improves fault detection and reduces clearing time during geomagnetic disturbances.
The results support the adoption of waveshape-based unblocking in transformers exposed to elevated GIC levels.

title: Ionospheric Dynamics and Its Impact on RF Applications During Superstorm Events

sentences.text: Modern technological systems, including those underpinning the global economy, are increasingly dependent on radio frequency (RF) communication systems - both ground-based and satellite-based.
Consequently, the need for reliable and resilient RF systems, particularly those providing precise positioning, navigation, and timing (PNT) services, has never been more critical.
However, the accuracy of RF systems can be compromised by both man-made issues - such as radio frequency interference - and natural disturbances like geomagnetic storms.

These storms alter the characteristics and distribution of ionospheric density, which can significantly affect RF propagation and disrupt applications, such as SATCOM communications and Global Navigation Satellite System (GNSS) navigation services.

In this paper, we investigate the impact of geomagnetic storm events occurring in May, August, and October 2024 on the performance of GNSS applications for users across low-, mid-, and high-latitude regions.
We utilize multi-instrument observations to identify the drivers and characterize the ionospheric disturbances during these events.
In particular, we assess the similarities and differences in the levels of ionospheric disturbances and its spatial distribution during these storm events.

Particularly, we examine the latitudinal distribution of these disturbances to determine whether the impacts are significant even in mid-latitudes, regions that are traditionally considered relatively calm.

title: Expanding GNSS Ground-Based Ionospheric Monitoring: Retrieving Absolute TEC from Low-Elevation Wideband Signals During May 2024 Geomagnetic Storm Period

sentences.text: Accurate estimation of ionospheric total electron content (TEC) is essential for improving global navigation satellite system (GNSS) performance and understanding space weather.
Our work investigates the use of wideband GNSS pseudorange data to recover low-elevation absolute TEC measurements, which are typically discarded due to high noise and multipath.
Wideband signals like GPS L5 offer improved code resolution and reduced noise, making them promising for single-frequency TEC retrieval.
Expanding the use of low-elevation wideband GNSS signals addresses a key limitation in ionospheric monitoring.
Conventional GNSS-based TEC observations often exclude signals below$15-30^{\circ}$elevation due to multipath and low SNR, resulting in substantial data loss.
This is particularly problematic in high-latitude regions, where ground-based receiver coverage is sparse and satellite visibility at high elevations is limited.
Our past work shows that noise in wideband pseudorange-derived TEC is significantly lower than that of narrowband signals, especially below 30° elevation.
However, hardware biases, a nuisance error in this process, need to be removed in order to retrieve absolute (unbiased) TEC.

title: Response of High-Latitude GNSS Scintillations to Ionospheric Gradients and Particle Precipitation During Storms and Substorms

sentences.text: Global Navigation Satellite System (GNSS) signals are highly susceptible to ionospheric scintillations, which can degrade positioning accuracy by several meters even under mild conditions and can cause total signal loss during periods of strong geomagnetic activity.

High-latitude regions are particularly affected due to enhanced particle precipitation and strong ionospheric convection, making these areas critical for both operational navigation systems and space weather forecasting.

This study examines the response of global scintillations during geomagnetic storms and substorms, using eight years (2013─2021) of amplitude (S4) and phase ($\sigma_{\phi}$) measurements from the Canadian High Arctic Ionospheric Network (CHAIN), providing extensive coverage across multiple geomagnetic latitudes and local times.
We find that scintillation response is largest during the storm main phase and the substorm expansion phase, highlighting the key role of transient geomagnetic activity.

The analysis considers all storm and substorm phases to characterize how temporal and spatial gradients of total electron content (TEC), together with particle precipitation, are linked to scintillations.

Statistical analysis, considering response times up to one hour after storm and substorm onsets, reveals significant correlations between TEC gradients and the$\sigma_{\phi}$index, particularly near dawn and noon magnetic local time at 70° magnetic latitude.
The response shifts poleward with increasing response time and exhibits discernible dawn─dusk asymmetries.
In addition, a persistent response develops in the convection throat, becoming noticeable after 10 minutes and possibly associated with polar cap patches and cusp precipitation.
Enhancement of scintillations is also observed at premidnight, likely associated with monoenergetic electron precipitation.

The observed density fluctuations that drive scintillations are likely generated by gradient drift instabilities in regions of strong convection, with Kelvin─Helmholtz instabilities potentially contributing in areas of strong flow shear.

The spatial distribution further suggests that diffuse electron precipitation contributes to dawn─dusk asymmetries, whereas enhanced electron density in the convection throat during storms likely drives the noon response.

By systematically linking TEC gradients, particle precipitation, and observed scintillation responses, this study provides new insight into the physical mechanisms controlling GNSS signal disturbances at high latitudes and their temporal evolution, with implications for both operational navigation systems and predictive space weather modeling.
